title: Understanding African Hair Texture
author: Qress-ent Team
excerpt: African hair is uniquely beautiful and diverse. Learning how it grows, coils and responds to care is the first step to treating it with the respect it deserves.
content:
African hair comes in a wide range of textures — from fine coils to tight, springy curls and everything in between. What unites many of these textures is a structure that is often more elliptical than round, which creates the beautiful spiral patterns we see.

Because of this structure, natural African hair tends to be more fragile along the length and can be prone to dryness. Moisture does not travel as easily from root to tip as it does in straighter hair types. This is not a flaw — it is simply how our hair is designed.

Understanding your own texture helps you choose the right products and routines. Some hair thrives with lightweight leave-ins, while denser coils may need richer creams and oils. The goal is never to change the nature of the hair, but to support it so it can remain strong, shiny and full of life.

At Qress-ent we believe that caring for African hair starts with knowledge and ends with confidence. When you understand your hair, you stop fighting it and start celebrating it.

title: Moisture & Scalp Care Basics
author: Qress-ent Team
excerpt: Healthy hair begins at the scalp. Simple, consistent moisture and gentle scalp care make a lasting difference for textured hair.
content:
Many people focus only on the length of their hair and forget the foundation — the scalp. A clean, nourished scalp creates the best environment for hair to grow and thrive.

For African hair, moisture is especially important. Because our hair can lose water more easily, regular hydration becomes a key part of any routine. This does not mean heavy products every day. It means listening to what your hair needs: sometimes a light mist, sometimes a deeper treatment.

Gentle cleansing is equally important. Over-washing can strip natural oils, while under-washing can lead to buildup. Finding a rhythm that keeps the scalp comfortable without dryness is the sweet spot.

Simple habits go a long way:
• Cleanse with care
• Moisturise consistently
• Protect hair at night
• Avoid excessive heat and tension

These small practices, done regularly, support both scalp health and the strength of the hair itself. At Qress-ent we create products with this daily reality in mind — care that feels natural, not complicated.

title: A Guide to Protective Hairstyles
author: Qress-ent Team
excerpt: Protective styles are more than a trend. They are a practical and beautiful way to care for African hair while honouring cultural traditions.
content:
Protective hairstyles have been part of African culture for centuries. Braids, twists, locs, cornrows and many other styles were never just about appearance — they were about protection, identity, community and practicality.

Today these styles continue to serve the same purpose. By keeping the ends of the hair tucked away and reducing daily manipulation, protective styles help retain length and minimise breakage. They also give us space to rest our hands from constant styling.

Popular protective styles include:
• Cornrows and single braids
• Twists (two-strand and flat twists)
• Locs and sisterlocs
• Bantu knots
• Wigs and weaves installed with care

The key to a successful protective style is balance. Styles that are too tight can cause tension and damage. Styles left in too long can lead to buildup or matting. Regular cleansing of the scalp, moisturising the hair underneath, and taking styles down gently are all part of healthy protective styling.

When done with care, protective styles become both a practical routine and a celebration of African hair artistry.

title: Traditional & Modern Interpretations
author: Qress-ent Team
excerpt: From classic cornrows to contemporary takes on ancient styles, African hairstyles continue to evolve while staying rooted in heritage.
content:
African hairstyles carry deep history. Different patterns, shapes and techniques once signalled age, status, community, marital status or spiritual beliefs. Cornrows, for example, have been documented for thousands of years across the continent.

Today we see these same foundations expressed in new ways. Classic cornrows may be combined with beads, coloured extensions or modern parting patterns. Locs are worn in freeform, cultivated or sculpted styles. Twists appear in endless variations of size and finish.

This evolution is not a loss of tradition — it is proof of its strength. Culture remains alive when it can move with the people who carry it. Young people reinvent old styles; older generations pass down techniques; artists and stylists push the boundaries of what is possible with textured hair.

At Qress-ent we celebrate both the traditional and the contemporary. Whether someone chooses a simple, low-maintenance style or an elaborate protective design, the common thread is pride in African hair and the stories it holds.

title: Hair as Identity & Heritage
author: Catherine & Tracy
excerpt: Our hair is never just hair. It carries memory, culture, resistance, beauty and belonging.
content:
For many of us, hair is one of the first ways we learn who we are. The hands that braided our hair as children, the comments we heard growing up, the first time we decided to wear our natural texture in public — these moments shape us.

Across Africa and the diaspora, hair has always been more than appearance. It has been a language. Styles could communicate identity, community and even resistance. During times when African features were devalued, choosing to wear natural hair or traditional styles became an act of self-affirmation.

Today the conversation continues. Some people are returning to their natural texture after years of chemical straightening. Others are exploring locs, braids or cuts that feel true to them. Each choice is personal, and each choice deserves respect.

At Qress-ent we hold a simple belief: hair is an identity. It is not something to be fixed or hidden. It is something to be understood, cared for and celebrated. When we honour our hair, we honour a part of ourselves and the generations that came before us.

title: From Qressinah to Qress-ent
author: Catherine & Tracy
excerpt: The story of how two sisters turned a shared love of African hair into a brand built on identity, care and heritage.
content:
Qress-ent did not begin as a big company. It began as Qressinah Enterprises — a small venture driven by two sisters who cared deeply about African hair and the people who wear it.

Catherine and Tracy Ojiambo grew up understanding that hair is personal. They saw how confidence could rise or fall with the state of someone’s hair. They also saw how few products and conversations truly centred African textures and experiences.

Over time the vision became clearer. The brand needed a name and identity that reflected its deeper purpose. That is how Qress-ent was born — an evolution of Qressinah Enterprises, still rooted in the same values, but with a stronger focus on identity, culture and care.

Today Qress-ent stands for a simple idea: hair is an identity. Everything we create, every story we share, and every product we offer is guided by that belief. We are still growing, still learning, and still committed to serving our community with honesty and warmth.

This is only the beginning of the journey.
